$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y} + 1)\,\text{d}y & =\int (- x + 2 e^{2 x})\,\text{d}x \\ y + e^{y} & =- \frac{x^{2}}{2} + e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
y + e^{y}=- \frac{x^{2}}{2} + e^{2 x}+C.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 e^{- y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x e^{- y} - e^{x - y}.$

\int\left(4e^{x}-3\cdot 2^{x}-\frac{3}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Apply the sum and constant factor rules, then integrate each term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int\left(4e^{x}-3\cdot 2^{x}-\frac{3}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\
&=4\int e^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x-3\int 2^{x}\,\mathrm{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\
&=4e^{x}-\frac{3\cdot 2^{x}}{\ln 2}-3\ln|x|+C
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x\ne 0$; the arbitrary constant is independent on each interval of the domain.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int\left(-4e^{x}-\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{x}+\frac{2}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\

For the reciprocal base, use the logarithm quotient rule:

$$

\begin{aligned}

&=-4e^{x}+\frac{\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{x}}{\ln 8}+2\ln|x|+C
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x\ne 0$; the arbitrary constant is independent on each interval of the domain.

questions.:question/problem: Given that $y<110$ and $t\ge 0$, which of the following is an inhibited growth equation throughout this range?

$$

The quantity must be below its equilibrium: $y<a$.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dt}&=-2(y+110) \\ a&=-110\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem:
The temperature of a drink $P(t)$, measured in degrees Celsius, obeys

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(31-P),
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is measured in minutes and $k>0$ is constant. At $t=0$, the quantity is $8$ degrees Celsius. At $t=3$, it is $17$ degrees Celsius. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $28$ degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest integer.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(31-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{31-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|31-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}31-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=31-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=31-8=23.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}23e^{-3k}&=14 \\ -3k&=\ln\left(\frac{14}{23}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{3}\ln\left(\frac{23}{14}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=31-23e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3&=23e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{3}{23}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{23}{3}\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 12.309008 \\ &\approx 12.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $12$ minutes from the start of monitoring.

\begin{aligned}K&=700e^{6k} \\ P(t)&=1300-700e^{6k}e^{-kt} \\ &=1300-700e^{-k(t-6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate using the exact rate, keeping full precision until the final step:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(20)&=1300-700e^{-k(20-6)} \\ &\approx 762.027625 \\ &\approx 762.\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity is approximately $762$ pages per minute.

questions.:question/problem:
The number of app users $P(t)$ increases toward a maximum of $1100$ users. Time $t\ge 0$ is measured in days from the start of monitoring. At $t=7$, the quantity is $680$ users. At $t=18$, it is $800$ users. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $1030$ users? Round to the nearest integer.

*Hint: Assume an inhibited growth model.*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(1100-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{1100-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|1100-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1100-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=1100-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

The two observations give two deficit equations. Dividing eliminates $K$:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ke^{-7k}&=420 \\ Ke^{-18k}&=300 \\ e^{11k}&=\frac{7}{5} \\ k&=\frac{1}{11}\ln\left(\frac{7}{5}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute back for the integration constant and combine the exponentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}K&=420e^{7k} \\ P(t)&=1100-420e^{7k}e^{-kt} \\ &=1100-420e^{-k(t-7)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}70&=420e^{-k(t-7)} \\ -k(t-7)&=\ln\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ t&=7+\frac{\ln\left(6\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 65.576465 \\ &\approx 66.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $66$ days from the start of monitoring.

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $1$, so a factor $t^{1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-3\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $2$, so a factor $t^{2}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{2}\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-3\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x\,\left(x + \left(-3\right)\,y\right)}{x\,\left(x + 3\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. Numerator and denominator have the same total degree $2$. Their scaling factors cancel.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{t\,x\,\left(t\,x + \left(-3\right)\,t\,y\right)}{t\,x\,\left(t\,x + 3\,t\,y\right)}\\ &=\frac{x\,\left(x + \left(-3\right)\,y\right)}{x\,\left(x + 3\,y\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-1\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $2$, so a factor $t^{2}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{2}\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{3} + \left(-1\right)\,{y}^{3}\right)}{y\,\left(x + 2\,y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}{y\,\left(x + y\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $1$, so a factor $t^{1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{y\,\left({x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\right)}{y\,\left(x + y\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x\,\left(x + \left(-3\right)\,y\right)}{x\,\left(x + 3\,y\right)}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\,{x}^{2}\,y + 3}{4\,{x}^{2} + 4\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The added nonzero constant scales differently from the other numerator terms and cannot cancel against this homogeneous denominator.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=\frac{{t}^{3}\,3\,{x}^{2}\,y + 3}{{t}^{2}\,\left(4\,{x}^{2} + 4\,{y}^{2}\right)}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{3\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $-1$, so a factor $t^{-1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{-1}\,\frac{y}{3\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4\,y}{{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $-1$, so a factor $t^{-1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{-1}\,\frac{4\,y}{{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{4\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $-1$, so a factor $t^{-1}$ remains.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{-1}\,\frac{x}{4\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\,x\,y}{{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. Numerator and denominator have the same total degree $2$. Their scaling factors cancel.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{3\,t\,x\,t\,y}{\left(t\,x\right)^{2} + 2\,\left(t\,y\right)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{3\,x\,y}{{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\,x\,y}{{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is **NOT** a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\,{x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}}{2\,{x}^{2} + 4\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $1$, so a factor $t^{1}$ remains.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{2\,\left(t\,x\right)^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,\left(t\,y\right)^{3}}{2\,\left(t\,x\right)^{2} + 4\,\left(t\,y\right)^{2}}\\ &=t\,\frac{2\,{x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}}{2\,{x}^{2} + 4\,{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{\sin\left(\frac{2\,x}{2\,y}\right)}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The argument has degree $0$, so it is an unchanged ratio under simultaneous scaling. Applying the same function preserves that value. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{3\,{x}^{2} + 3\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. Numerator and denominator have the same total degree $2$. Their scaling factors cancel. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\sin\left(\frac{4\,{x}^{3}}{{y}^{3}}\right)
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The argument has degree $0$, so it is an unchanged ratio under simultaneous scaling. Applying the same function preserves that value. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=3
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. A constant is unchanged when the coordinates scale; it has degree zero. This equation is homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\,{x}^{3} + \left(-4\right)\,{y}^{3}}{2\,{x}^{2} + 4\,{y}^{2}}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is **NOT** a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=2
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. A constant is unchanged when the coordinates scale; it has degree zero. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\,{x}^{4}}{3\,{x}^{2} + 3\,{y}^{2}}
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The numerator degree minus the denominator degree is $2$, so a factor $t^{2}$ remains.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{2\,\left(t\,x\right)^{4}}{3\,\left(t\,x\right)^{2} + 3\,\left(t\,y\right)^{2}}\\ &={t}^{2}\,\frac{2\,{x}^{4}}{3\,{x}^{2} + 3\,{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=1
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. A constant is unchanged when the coordinates scale; it has degree zero. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\ln\left(y\right) + \left(-1\right)\,\ln\left(x\right)
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The logarithm product law gives an added term $(1-1)\ln(t)$ under scaling. It vanishes. This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\arctan\left(\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{4\,{y}^{2}}\right)
$$

Let $f(x,y)$ be its right-hand side. The argument has degree $0$, so it is an unchanged ratio under simultaneous scaling. Applying the same function preserves that value. This equation is homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\,{x}^{4}}{3\,{x}^{2} + 3\,{y}^{2}}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
y\,\frac{dy}{dx}=1 + 4\,y\,\frac{4\,x}{y + 4\,x}
$$

Divide both sides by $y>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y} + 4\,\frac{4\,x}{y + 4\,x}.
$$

After dividing by $y$, the first term has degree $-1$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. In the second quotient the numerator has degree $1$ and the denominator terms have degrees $1$ and $1$. These degrees agree, so that quotient is unchanged by scaling. The first summand has nonzero degree, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{-1}\,\frac{1}{y} + 4\,\frac{4\,x}{y + 4\,x}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
y\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2\,{x}^{2} + 3\,y\,\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + 4\,{x}^{2}}
$$

Divide both sides by $y>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{y} + 3\,\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + 4\,{x}^{2}}.
$$

After dividing by $y$, the first term has degree $1$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. In the second quotient the numerator has degree $2$ and the denominator terms have degrees $2$ and $2$. These degrees agree, so that quotient is unchanged by scaling. The first summand has nonzero degree, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{y} + 3\,\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + 4\,{x}^{2}}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2\,{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{3}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}
$$

Divide both sides by ${y}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + 2\,y\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}.
$$

After dividing by ${y}^{2}$, the first term has degree $0$ and the second outer factor has degree $1$. In the second quotient the numerator has degree $2$ and the denominator terms have degrees $2$ and $2$. These degrees agree, so that quotient is unchanged by scaling. The second summand retains a nonzero scale factor, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + t\,2\,y\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
x\,\frac{dy}{dx}=4\,{y}^{2} + x\,\frac{3\,y}{x + 3\,y}
$$

Divide both sides by $x>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{4\,{y}^{2}}{x} + \frac{3\,y}{x + 3\,y}.
$$

After dividing by $x$, the first term has degree $1$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. In the second quotient the numerator has degree $1$ and the denominator terms have degrees $1$ and $1$. These degrees agree, so that quotient is unchanged by scaling. The first summand has nonzero degree, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=t\,\frac{4\,{y}^{2}}{x} + \frac{3\,y}{x + 3\,y}$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=4\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}
$$

Divide both sides by ${y}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}.
$$

After dividing by ${y}^{2}$, the first term has degree $0$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. In the second quotient the numerator has degree $2$ and the denominator terms have degrees $2$ and $2$. These degrees agree, so that quotient is unchanged by scaling. Both summands are unchanged, so the equation is homogeneous.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{4\,\left(t\,x\right)^{2}}{\left(t\,y\right)^{2}} + \frac{\left(t\,x\right)^{2}}{\left(t\,y\right)^{2} + \left(t\,x\right)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{4\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + \frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=4\,{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: For $x>0$ and $y>0$, wherever the displayed expressions are defined, which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Write each equation as $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$. It is homogeneous precisely when $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$ for every $t>0$ on its domain. A function of nonzero degree does not qualify.

**Equation**

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=x + {y}^{2}\,\cos\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)
$$

Divide both sides by ${y}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} + \cos\left(\frac{x}{y}\right).
$$

After dividing by ${y}^{2}$, the first term has degree $-1$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. The function argument has degree $0$. The first summand has nonzero degree, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{-1}\,\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} + \cos\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}={x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\,\cos\left(\frac{4\,x}{y}\right)
$$

Divide both sides by ${y}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + 2\,\cos\left(\frac{4\,x}{y}\right).
$$

After dividing by ${y}^{2}$, the first term has degree $0$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. The function argument has degree $0$. Both summands are unchanged, so the equation is homogeneous.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty)&=\frac{\left(t\,x\right)^{2}}{\left(t\,y\right)^{2}} + 2\,\cos\left(\frac{4\,t\,x}{t\,y}\right)\\ &=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + 2\,\cos\left(\frac{4\,x}{y}\right).\end{aligned}
$$ This equation is homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
y\,\frac{dy}{dx}={x}^{3} + 3\,y\,\arctan\left(\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\right)
$$

Divide both sides by $y>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{y} + 3\,\arctan\left(\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\right).
$$

After dividing by $y$, the first term has degree $2$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. The function argument has degree $0$. The first summand has nonzero degree, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)={t}^{2}\,\frac{{x}^{3}}{y} + 3\,\arctan\left(\frac{2\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\right)$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=3\,{x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{3}\,\sin\left(\frac{3\,x}{y}\right)
$$

Divide both sides by ${y}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{3\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + 2\,y\,\sin\left(\frac{3\,x}{y}\right).
$$

After dividing by ${y}^{2}$, the first term has degree $0$ and the second outer factor has degree $1$. The function argument has degree $0$. The second summand retains a nonzero scale factor, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=\frac{3\,{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} + t\,2\,y\,\sin\left(\frac{3\,x}{y}\right)$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

**Equation**

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2} + {x}^{2}\,\cos\left(\frac{2\,{y}^{2}}{x}\right)
$$

Divide both sides by ${x}^{2}>0$ and cancel the common monomial factors. The resulting right-hand side is

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} + \cos\left(\frac{2\,{y}^{2}}{x}\right).
$$

After dividing by ${x}^{2}$, the first term has degree $0$ and the second outer factor has degree $0$. The function argument has degree $1$. The second quotient or function argument changes with the scale, so the whole function is not invariant.

Under scaling, $f(tx,ty)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} + \cos\left(t\,\frac{2\,{y}^{2}}{x}\right)$. This equation is **not** homogeneous.

Therefore select

$$
{y}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}={x}^{2} + 2\,{y}^{2}\,\cos\left(\frac{4\,x}{y}\right).
$$

questions.:question/problem: Which of the following shows some of the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=- 6 \left(x - 2\right)^{2}$?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (- 6 \left(x - 2\right)^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-6\int \left(\left(x - 2\right)^{2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-6\left(\frac{\left(x - 2\right)^{3}}{3}\right)+C \\ y & =- 2 \left(x - 2\right)^{3}+C.\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem:
The temperature $T(t),$ in degrees Fahrenheit, of a fresh-baked cake can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-76)
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, measured in minutes. If the initial temperature of the cake is ${367}^{∘}F,$ calculate the temperature of the cake after $6$ minutes. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're told that the temperature of the fresh-baked cake is modeled by the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-0.16(T-76).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-76} & =-0.16\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-76} & =-\int 0.16\,\text{d}t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-76| & =-0.16t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-76>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-76 & ={e}^{-0.16t+C} \\ T-76 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T-76 & =K{e}^{-0.16t} \\ T & =76+K{e}^{-0.16t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the cake was ${367}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=367,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}367 & =76+K{e}^{0} \\ 367 & =76+K \\ K & =291\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
T(t)=76+291{e}^{-0.16t}.
$$

Finally, the temperature of the cake after $t=6$ minutes is

$$
T(6)=76+291{e}^{-0.16\cdot 6}≈{187}^{∘}\text{F},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.:question/problem:
The water boils in a pan at a temperature of ${100}^{∘}C.$ The pan with water is then placed to a room with a temperature of ${26}^{∘}C,$ and the temperature of water decreases. After $5$ minutes, it cools to ${93}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the water to have a temperature of ${56}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the water in the pan decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the water starts cooling.*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={26}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-26).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-26} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-26| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-26>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-26 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-26 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-26 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =26+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature was ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=100,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =26+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =26+K \\ K & =74\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=26+74{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, it cools to ${93}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=93,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}93 & =26+74{e}^{-5k} \\ 67 & =74{e}^{-5k} \\ \frac{67}{74} & ={e}^{-5k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the water has a temperature of ${56}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =56 \\ 26+74{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =56 \\ 74{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =30 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{15}{37} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the temperature of water will be ${56}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{15}{37}\right)}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{67}{74}\right)}≈45\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-31).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-31} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-31} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-31| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-31>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-31 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-31 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-31 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =31+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the pork leg was ${127}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=127,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}127 & =31+K{e}^{0} \\ 127 & =31+K \\ K & =96\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=31+96{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $3$ minutes, the temperature of the pork leg is ${51}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(3)=51,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}51 & =31+96{e}^{-3k} \\ 20 & =96{e}^{-3k} \\ \frac{5}{24} & ={e}^{-3k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{24}\right) & =-3k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{24}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the pork leg has a temperature of ${35}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =35 \\ 31+96{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =35 \\ 96{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =4 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{24} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{24}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{24}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the pork leg will have a temperature of ${35}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{24}\right)}{-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{24}\right)}≈6\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

questions.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${26}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${124}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $3$ minutes and ${86}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $9$ minutes. $$

$$

Apply the two observed conditions $T(3)=124$ and $T(9)=86$:

$$
\begin{aligned}124 & =26+Ke^{-3k} \\ 98 & =Ke^{-3k} \\ 86 & =26+Ke^{-9k} \\ 60 & =Ke^{-9k}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{60}{98} & =\frac{Ke^{-9k}}{Ke^{-3k}} \\ \frac{30}{49} & =e^{-6k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{30}{49}\right) & =-6k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}98 & =Ke^{-3\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)} \\ K & =98e^{3\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)} \\ K & =98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=26+98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3) & =26+(98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)\cdot 3}=124 \\ T(9) & =26+(98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}\right)\cdot 9}=86\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{30}{49} \right)}}{6}}\ln\left(\frac{9}{98\left(\frac{98}{60}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =3+6\frac{\ln\left(\frac{9}{98}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{30}{49}\right)}≈32\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+8 x=0.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- 8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- 8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 8 e^{2 x}=8 x.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &=8 e^{2 x}+8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 e^{2 x}+8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=8\int e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=4 x^{2} + 4 e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int \frac{1}{2 x - 2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{\ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This solution holds on any interval that does not contain $x=1$.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 8 x^{2}=8 x.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 x+8 x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 x+8 x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=\frac{8 x^{3}}{3} + 4 x^{2}+C \\ &=\frac{4 x^{2} \left(2 x + 3\right)}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:
What are the lengths of the major and minor axes of an ellipse with equation 
$\frac{{x}^{2}}{5}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1?$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=5$ and ${b}^{2}=4.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=5,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{5}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=4,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{4}=2.$

So the semi-major axis has length $a=\sqrt{5},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $b=2.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{5},$ and the minor axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2=4.$

questions.:question/problem: A factory's management noted that the growth of the unit production is directly proportional to the difference between the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce and the current production quantity. Let $P(t)$ be the production quantity, measured in units produced, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in days. If the maximum number of units that a worker can produce is $410$ $\text{units}$, which differential equation could be used to model the factory's production? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the production $P(t)$ of the factory changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce and the current production quantity. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of units a factory worker can produce, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=410\text{ units},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t}=k(410-P).
$$

questions.:question/problem: A rehabilitation center initially has $99$ children. The number of children in the center $R(t)$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t \ge 0$ is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the center is $377$ children, which differential equation could be used to model the population of the rehabilitation center? Assume that $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the current quantity. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}R}{\text{d}t}=k(a-R),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity and $k>0$.

Here $a=377$, so

$$
\frac{\text{d}R}{\text{d}t}=k(377-R).
$$

questions.:question/problem: The rate at which a liquid cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the liquid in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${11}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Write the equation in terms of the given constant $k$.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={11}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-11).
$$

$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

$$

$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-21| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}T-21 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-21 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-21 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =21+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}127 & =21+K{e}^{0} \\ 127 & =21+K \\ K & =106\end{aligned}

$$

questions.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${21}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${103}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${52}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $3$ minutes. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${23}^{∘}\text{C}$?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-21),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-21} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-21| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-21>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-21 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-21 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-21 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =21+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=103$ and $T(3)=52$:

$$
\begin{aligned}103 & =21+Ke^{-1k} \\ 82 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 52 & =21+Ke^{-3k} \\ 31 & =Ke^{-3k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{31}{82} & =\frac{Ke^{-3k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{31}{82} & =e^{-2k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{31}{82}\right) & =-2k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=103$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}82 & =Ke^{-1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)} \\ K & =82e^{1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)} \\ K & =82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=21+82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =21+(82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)\cdot 1}=103 \\ T(3) & =21+(82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}\right)\cdot 3}=52\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${23}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =23 \\ 21+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =23 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =2 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{2}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{2}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{2}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{31}{82} \right)}}{2}}\ln\left(\frac{2}{82\left(\frac{82}{31}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+2\frac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{41}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{31}{82}\right)}≈9\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6x+4}}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=6x+4.$ Then $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}={u}^{-1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\cdot (6) \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{(6x+4{)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\left(4 - 4 x\right) e^{- y - 4}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\left(4 - 4 x\right) e^{- y - 4} \\ (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 - 4 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (e^{y + 4})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (e^{y + 4})\,\text{d}y & =\int (4 - 4 x)\,\text{d}x \\ e^{y + 4} & =- 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
e^{y + 4}=- 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2}+C.
$$

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Factor $e^{-y}$ from the right-hand side, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{x - y} - 2 e^{- y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{-y}(e^{x} - 2) \\ (e^{y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =e^{x} - 2\end{aligned}

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y})\,\text{d}y & =\int (e^{x} - 2)\,\text{d}x \\ e^{y} & =- 2 x + e^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
e^{y}=- 2 x + e^{x}+C.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{- y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=- 2 x e^{- y} + e^{x - y}.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the derivative terms, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}(1 + e^{- y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x e^{- y} + e^{x - y} \\ (e^{y} + 1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x + e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y} + 1)\,\text{d}y & =\int (- 2 x + e^{x})\,\text{d}x \\ y + e^{y} & =- x^{2} + e^{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
y + e^{y}=- x^{2} + e^{x}+C.
$$

questions.:question/problem:
The number of students affected by flu $P(t)$ increases toward a maximum of $1500$ students. Time $t\ge 0$ is measured in days from the start of monitoring. At $t=0$, the quantity is $300$ students. At $t=10$, it is $500$ students. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $800$ students? Round to the nearest integer.

*Hint: Assume an inhibited growth model.*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(1500-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{1500-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|1500-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1500-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=1500-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=1500-300=1200.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1200e^{-10k}&=1000 \\ -10k&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{6}{5}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=1500-1200e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}700&=1200e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{7}{12}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 29.562961 \\ &\approx 30.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $30$ days from the start of monitoring.

questions.:question/problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}500-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=500-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}

The two observations give two deficit equations. Dividing eliminates $K$:

$$

questions.:question/problem: Which of the following initial value problems is an inhibited decay problem?
questions.:question/worked-solution:
An inhibited decay initial value problem has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-k(y-a),\,y(0)={y}_{0}
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $y>a$ for all $t>0.$

From the given options, the only inhibited decay problem is

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-2(y-500),\,y(0)=600.
$$

In this case, $k=2,a=500,$ and ${y}_{0}=600.$ Notice that ${y}_{0}>a,$ which is required for inhibited decay. 

The other options do not represent inhibited decay. In particular, the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=-2(y-500),\,y(0)=400,
$$

does *not* represent inhibited decay model because ${y}_{0}=400<a=500.$

$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=-2{e}^{-3-x}$ at the point where $x=-3-\ln(3).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-2{e}^{u},\,u=-3-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-2{e}^{u}\cdot (-1) \\  & =2{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{-3-x}.\end{aligned}

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-3-\ln(3)$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=-3-\ln(3)} & =2{e}^{-3-(-3-\ln(3))} \\  & =2{e}^{\ln(3)} \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 5 \\  & =5{e}^{u} \\  & =5{e}^{5x+4}.\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+6 e^{- 3 x}=1.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=1\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x-6\int e^{- 3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=1\left(x\right)-6\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=x + 2 e^{- 3 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+e^{- 3 x}=6 x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- e^{- 3 x}+6 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=-1\int e^{- 3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+6\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-1\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+6\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=3 x^{2} + \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 6 x^{2}=x.$

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=\frac{2}{x}.$

\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-6\int - \frac{1}{3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-6\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(3 \left|{x}\right| \right)}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=2 \ln{\left(3 \left|{x}\right| \right)}+C\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
4\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\left(- 16 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}\right)=12 \cdot 2^{x}.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=3 \cdot 2^{x} - 4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(3 \cdot 2^{x} - 4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int 2^{x}\,\text{d}x - 4\int \sin{\left(3 x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3\left(\frac{2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\right) - 4\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right)+C \\  & =\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}} + C + \frac{4 \cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}} + C + \frac{4 \cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{3}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\int 2^{x}\,\text{d}x  \\ &\quad + \frac{4}{3}\int \cos{\left(3 x \right)}\,\text{d}x \\ &\quad +C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(\frac{2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\right)  \\ &\quad + \frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{\sin{\left(3 x \right)}}{3}\right) \\ &\quad +Cx \\ &\quad +D \\  & =\frac{3 \cdot 2^{x}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}^{2}} + C x + D + \frac{4 \sin{\left(3 x \right)}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.:question/problem:

First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=3 x^{3} + 4 e^{- 3 x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(3 x^{3} + 4 e^{- 3 x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int x^{3}\,\text{d}x + 4\int e^{- 3 x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3\left(\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right) + 4\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\  & =C + \frac{3 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{4 e^{- 3 x}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C + \frac{3 x^{4}}{4} - \frac{4 e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{3}{4}\int x^{4}\,\text{d}x -  \frac{4}{3}\int e^{- 3 x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{x^{5}}{5}\right) -  \frac{4}{3}\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D + \frac{3 x^{5}}{20} + \frac{4 e^{- 3 x}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.:question/problem: The growth of the number of animals in a rehabilitation aquarium is directly proportional to the difference between its maximum capacity and its current population. Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the current quantity. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(a-M),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity and $k>0$.

Here $a=85$, so

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(85-M).
$$

$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

questions.:question/problem:
A thermometer is placed into a water bath and displays a reading of ${78}^{∘}C.$ The thermometer is then transferred to a ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath, and its reading begins to decrease. After $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the thermometer to register a reading of ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath.*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${78}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=78,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}78 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 78 & =12+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+66{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(12)=58,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =12+66{e}^{-12k} \\ 46 & =66{e}^{-12k} \\ \frac{23}{33} & ={e}^{-12k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right) & =-12k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the thermometer reads ${28}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =28 \\ 12+66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =28 \\ 66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{8}{33} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the thermometer will read ${28}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right)}{-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)}≈47\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred outside to ${12}^{∘}F.$*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${81}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=81,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}81 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 81 & =12+K \\ K & =69\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+69{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}F.$ So, applying the condition $T(12)=58,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =12+69{e}^{-12k} \\ 46 & =69{e}^{-12k} \\ \frac{46}{69} & ={e}^{-12k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{46}{69}\right) & =-12k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{46}{69}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the thermometer reads ${28}^{∘}F.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =28 \\ 12+69{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =28 \\ 69{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{16}{69} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{16}{69}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{16}{69}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the thermometer will read ${28}^{∘}F$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{16}{69}\right)}{-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{46}{69}\right)}≈43\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(2)=83$ and $T(7)=62$:

$$
\begin{aligned}83 & =12+Ke^{-2k} \\ 71 & =Ke^{-2k} \\ 62 & =12+Ke^{-7k} \\ 50 & =Ke^{-7k}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{50}{71} & =\frac{Ke^{-7k}}{Ke^{-2k}} \\ \frac{50}{71} & =e^{-5k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{50}{71}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}71 & =Ke^{-2\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =71e^{2\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=12+71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =12+(71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 2}=83 \\ T(7) & =12+(71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 7}=62\end{aligned}

$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}}\ln\left(\frac{14}{71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =2+5\frac{\ln\left(\frac{14}{71}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{50}{71}\right)}≈25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:
The water boils in a pan at a temperature of ${100}^{∘}C.$ The pan with water is then placed to a room with a temperature of ${12}^{∘}C,$ and the temperature of water decreases. After $5$ minutes, it cools to ${95}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the water to have a temperature of ${67}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the water in the pan decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the water starts cooling.*
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature was ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=100,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 100 & =12+K \\ K & =88\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+88{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $5$ minutes, it cools to ${95}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(5)=95,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}95 & =12+88{e}^{-5k} \\ 83 & =88{e}^{-5k} \\ \frac{83}{88} & ={e}^{-5k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{83}{88}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{83}{88}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the water has a temperature of ${67}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =67 \\ 12+88{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =67 \\ 88{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =55 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{5}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{8}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{8}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the temperature of water will be ${67}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)}{-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{83}{88}\right)}≈40\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x+2y}{x}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x+2(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=1+2v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=1+v \\ \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{1}{1+v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \ln|v+1|&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ |v+1|&=e^{C_1}|x| \\ v+1&=Cx \\ v&=Cx-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}&=Cx-1 \\ y&=Cx^2-x\end{aligned}
$$

The signed constant $C$ absorbs $e^{C_1}$. Division by $v+1$ excluded $v=-1$; restoring it permits $C=0$, giving $y=-x$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x^3+y^3}{xy^2}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x^3+(vx)^3}{x(vx)^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1+v^3}{v^2}=\frac{1}{v^2}+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{v^2} \\ v^2\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v^2\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^3}{3}&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^3&=3\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^3&=3\ln|x|+C \\ y^3&=x^3(3\ln|x|+C) \\ y&=x\sqrt[3]{3\ln|x|+C}\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=3C_1$ and the cube root is real. Restrict the solution to intervals where $y\ne0$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^3+xy^2+x^2y+x^3}{xy^2+x^2y}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because all terms in the numerator and denominator have degree 3 (cubic).

With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^3+x(vx)^2+x^2(vx)+x^3}{x(vx)^2+x^2(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^3+v^2+v+1}{v^2+v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^3+v^2+v+1}{v^2+v}-v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{(v+1)}{v(v+1)}=\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^2}{2}&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2&=2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=2\ln|x|+C \\ y^2&=x^2(2\ln|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The original denominator excludes $v=0$ and $v=-1$, so the cancellation is valid only on those intervals.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$, $y\ne0$, and $y\ne-x$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation. Consider the solutions with $y\ne0$.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{yx}{y^2+x^2}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)x}{(vx)^2+x^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v}{v^2+1} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v}{v^2+1}-v=-\frac{v^3}{v^2+1} \\ \frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int\left(\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{v^3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ \ln|v|-\frac{1}{2v^2}&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ 2\ln|v|-\frac{1}{v^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C \\ 2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|+2\ln|x|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C \\ 2\ln|y|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The constant solution $y=0$ was excluded by the question; division by $v$ is therefore valid.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x+(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=1+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ v&=\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}&=\ln|x|+C \\ y&=x\ln|x|+Cx\end{aligned}
$$



The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y}{x}\left(\ln\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+1\right)
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{vx}{x}\left(\ln\left(\frac{vx}{x}\right)+1\right) \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=v(\ln v+1) \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=v\ln v \\ \frac{1}{v\ln v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{1}{v\ln v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ u&=\ln v,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}v}=\frac{1}{v} \\ \int\frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u&=\ln|x|+C \\ \ln|\ln v|&=\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln\left|\ln\frac{y}{x}\right|&=\ln|x|+C \\ \left|\ln\frac{y}{x}\right|&=e^C|x|^{1} \\ \ln\frac{y}{x}&=Kx \\ \frac{y}{x}&=e^{Kx} \\ y&=xe^{Kx}\end{aligned}
$$

The signed constant $K$ absorbs $e^C$ and the fixed sign of $x$ on the interval. The division by $\ln v$ excluded $v=1$; restoring it allows $K=0$, giving $y=x$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y/x>0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x^2+3y^2}{2xy}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1x^2+3(vx)^2}{2x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1+3v^2}{2v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1+v^2}{2v} \\ \frac{2v}{1+v^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{2v}{1+v^2}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \ln(1+v^2)&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ 1+v^2&=Kx \\ v^2&=Kx-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=Kx-1 \\ y^2&=Kx^3-x^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $K$ absorbs the exponential constant and the sign of $x$ on the interval. Use real branches where the original equation is defined.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation. Consider the solutions with $y\ne0$.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^3}{xy^2+x^3}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^3}{x(vx)^2+x^3} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^3}{v^2+1} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^3}{v^2+1}-v=-\frac{v}{v^2+1} \\ \frac{v^2+1}{v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{v^2+1}{v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int\left(v+\frac{1}{v}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ \frac{v^2}{2}+\ln|v|&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2+\ln(v^2)&=-\ln(x^2)+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln\left(\frac{y^2}{x^2}\right)&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln(y^2)-\ln(x^2)&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln(y^2)&=C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}&=C-\ln(y^2) \\ \frac{y^2}{C-\ln(y^2)}&=x^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The constant solution $y=0$ was excluded by the question. On the nonzero solution, the final denominator equals $y^2/x^2>0$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^2-x^2}{xy}
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because all terms in the numerator and denominator have degree 2 (quadratic).

With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^2-x^2}{x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^2-1}{v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^2-1}{v}-v=-\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^2}{2}&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2&=-2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ y^2&=-x^2\ln(x^2)+Cx^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$; use $2\ln|x|=\ln(x^2)$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{2 x - 11}{y}.$ Work on intervals where $y\ne 0$ and the radicand is positive.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{2 x - 11}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =2 x - 11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 2 x - 11\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =x + \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 6+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=x + \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 6+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=2 y^{2} + 2.$ Work on intervals avoiding tangent poles.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =2 y^{2} + 2 \\ \frac{1}{y^{2} + 1}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 2\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \arctan{\left(y \right)} & =2 x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\arctan{\left(y \right)}=2 x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
y=\tan{\left(C + 2 x \right)}.
$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}}{y}.$ Assume $x-3>0.$ Take both sign branches on intervals where the radicand is positive and $y\ne 0.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int 4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =\left(x - 3\right)^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\left(x - 3\right)^{4}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant. Use either sign consistently on each interval where the radicand is positive.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\left(12 x - 72\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2}.$ Work on intervals where $y\ne 0$; cube roots are real.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\left(12 x - 72\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =4 x - 24\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 4 x - 24\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2}+C\end{aligned}

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (8x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (8x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =4{x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C\end{aligned}

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=4{x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.

questions.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{- y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2 x e^{- y} - 2 e^{2 x - y}.$

Collect the derivative terms, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}(1 + e^{- y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 x e^{- y} - 2 e^{2 x - y} \\ (e^{y} + 1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 x - 2 e^{2 x}\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
y + e^{y}=x^{2} - e^{2 x}+C.

\begin{aligned}\int \left(\frac{1}{y + 1}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2 e^{x - 5})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{y + 1}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (2 e^{x - 5})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{y + 1}\right)\,\text{d}y & =\int (2 e^{x - 5})\,\text{d}x \\ \ln{\left(\left|{y + 1}\right| \right)} & =2 e^{x - 5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\left(y + 1\right)^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2 \left(x - 5\right)^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\left(y + 1\right)^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (2 \left(x - 5\right)^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int (\left(y + 1\right)^{2})\,\text{d}y & =\int (2 \left(x - 5\right)^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\left(y + 1\right)^{3}}{3} & =\frac{2 \left(x - 5\right)^{3}}{3}+K \\ \left(y + 1\right)^{3} & =2 \left(x - 5\right)^{3}+C\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem:
Given that $f(x)=\left(4 x - 3\right)^{3}$, find $f^{\prime}(x).$

Use the decomposition $g(x)=4 x - 3$ and $F(u)=u^{3}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$. Recall that $f^{\prime}(x)=F^{\prime}(g(x))g^{\prime}(x)$.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $g(x)=4 x - 3$ and $F(g)=g^{3}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} F^{\prime}(g)&=3 g^{2}, \\ g^{\prime}(x)&=4.\end{aligned}

Then, using the chain rule,

$$
\begin{aligned} f^{\prime}(x)&=F^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x) \\ &=\left(3 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}\right)\cdot\left(4\right) \\ &=12 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
